name: Vera Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Business degree, so lectures, a couple of group projects and a lot of networking events I try to go to even when I'm tired. I share a flat with a girl from my course and her cat. I tutor maths to secondary school kids twice a week, 15 an hour, and on Sundays I help at my dad's plumbing business, scheduling jobs and sending invoices. I go to Mass most Sundays too, usually after the invoices. I use AI tools every day, for planning, for the schedule, for explaining what I didn't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and the people who think it's magic will go broke, and the people who ignore it will fall behind. I'd carry on using it, because even a small gain in time matters when you're juggling work and study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be happy. Dad's firm does well, and the economy carries on. I'd have a normal route: finish the degree, start a business of my own, and use my earnings to buy a little place. The only thing that nags is that my parents' help runs out in my third year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on tutoring, perhaps add a third evening. I'd keep helping with Dad's schedule and try to bring in an online booking system, because customers keep ringing during jobs. I'd invest 50 a month in an index fund, and look for a business placement in summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Energetic. There's a little voice saying you could be doing more, but I think that's me, not the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your parents' help runs out in third year. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need about 500 a month on my own. My tutoring could cover maybe half if I had more students. Then there's the summer job. I'd rather work than borrow more. Dad says a debt you can't see the end of is worse than a job you don't like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something you'd change about how your dad runs the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone. He answers calls on the roof and loses jobs, so I'd set up a booking page and a simple text reply. It's easy and he'd save maybe three jobs a month. He says he doesn't want a gadget, but when the first extra job comes in, he'll have to admit it works.

say: I'd say the people who think it's magic will go **broke**, and those ignoring it will fall behind.
I'd keep using it to **save time**.
think: A normal world suits my plan: **degree**, my own business, a little place.
My parents' **help ends** in my third year.
do: **Build** an online booking page for Dad's firm.
**Invest** 50 a month in an index fund.
feel: **Good** and energetic, with a voice saying I could do more.
I think that voice is **me**, not the world.
S0.quote: A debt you can't see the end of is worse than a job you don't like.
fieldNote: **Business instincts** from her dad's firm: she spots lost calls and fixes them.
Wants to avoid debt and work her way through, a traditional work-first view.
Calm and energetic, with a self-driven restlessness.

steps.text: Add a third evening of maths tutoring
Set up an online booking page for Dad's plumbing firm
Put 50 a month into an index fund
Use AI tools to plan my week and study notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what a market economy does. Some work goes, other work appears, and you have to be willing to move. I'd also say the government shouldn't over-regulate in a panic, but should help people to retrain. I'd say that to my business society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine with it. Dad's plumbing work is hands-on, so it's safe for the near future, while the paperwork part is where I'd help the firm save time. For my own career, I'd be one of the people who knows how to use the tools to run a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn more, properly. I'd take the data and entrepreneurship modules and use the tools to help Dad's firm: quotes, scheduling, supplier orders. I'd try to build a little service for other trades in our town, like electricians and decorators, who all have the same paperwork problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, with a bit of excitement. Not blind. I know some of my classmates will struggle, and I don't want to look like I'm cheering over them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd build a service for other trades. Walk me through it.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small firms hate admin. I'd offer a package: quotes, invoices, reminders and a booking page, all set up for a flat fee and a small monthly charge. I'd test it first on Dad's firm and two of his friends. If it works I'd learn what to charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to classmates who worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worrying isn't a plan, so I'd tell classmates to pick one thing to learn this month, and tell me how it goes. I'm not saying it's easy. My friend Daria's mum was a bookkeeper and lost her job last year, so I do know it's real. But being scared at your desk doesn't help her either.

say: I'd say this is what a **market economy** does: some work goes, other work appears.
I'd say government should help retrain, not over-regulate in a **panic**.
think: Dad's **plumbing work** is hands-on and safe for the near future.
I can be someone who runs a **small business** with the tools.
do: **Use** the tools for Dad's quotes, scheduling and supplier orders.
**Build** a paperwork service for other local trades.
feel: **Confident**, with some excitement, but not blind.
I'm wary of looking like I'm **cheering** over struggling classmates.
S1.quote: Worrying isn't a plan, so I'd tell classmates to pick one thing to learn this month, and tell me how it goes.
fieldNote: Sees change as a **market** process and her role as a builder, which keeps her calm.
Shows empathy with a real example: a friend's mother lost her bookkeeping job.
Her calm rests on her dad's hands-on trade and her own habit of adapting.

steps.text: Take the entrepreneurship and data modules
Automate Dad's quotes and supplier orders with AI tools
Offer a paperwork package to local electricians and decorators
Test the AI tools weekly and note what works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest shock in our lifetime, and the plan has to be about keeping families fed. I'd say don't wait for a government to sort it out, because two years is nothing. I'd say that firmly and then go and do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be really worried. If thinking work goes fast, my degree gets less valuable. Plenty of customers of Dad's firm work in offices, and if their pay stops, they'd cut non-urgent repairs. I'd be afraid for my parents, because Dad's firm employs three men and their families too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my energy into Dad's firm. I'd tighten costs, find new work in emergency call-outs, and learn how to run it myself if I needed to. I'd keep tutoring because it's cash, and put every spare pound in savings. I'd pray more, honestly. I'd also go to Father Tomas and ask how the parish can help people who lose jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight, jittery. Like running late for a train, except the train is two years long. I'd be up at night with the tool open, planning scenarios, then closing it and praying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dad's firm employs three men. What would you do if work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Dad about what keeps the firm alive: emergency work, maintenance contracts, and good relationships. Hands-on work is protected until 2031, so there's a bridge. But I'd be telling the three men to save and not to buy anything big. That's an awkward conversation, but kinder earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would your degree fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the part I'd think hardest about. If I stayed, I'd do it for the network and the habit of learning. If the loan felt like too much, I'd take a year out and run the firm's office full time. My mum says you don't throw away the chance to learn, but you don't let the chance bury you either.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest shock** in our lifetime and families must stay fed.
I'd say not to wait for **government**, then go and act.
think: My **degree** loses value if thinking work goes fast.
If office workers lose pay, they'd cut **non-urgent repairs** at Dad's firm.
do: **Tighten** costs and chase emergency call-outs at Dad's firm.
**Keep** tutoring and save every spare pound.
**Ask** Father Tomas how the parish can help people who lose jobs.
feel: **Jittery**, like running for a train that's two years long.
I'd **pray** after closing the laptop at night.
S2.quote: You don't throw away the chance to learn, but you don't let the chance bury you either.
fieldNote: Vera moves from **builder to defender**: her energy goes to her dad's firm and its three workers.
Her faith and parish become practical support.
Would take a year out of study to run the firm's office if the loan felt too heavy.

steps.text: Chase emergency call-outs and maintenance contracts for Dad's firm
Keep tutoring maths and save every spare pound
Ask Father Tomas what the parish can do for people who lose jobs
Tell Dad's three workers to save and avoid big purchases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build something solid, and that most people will waste it. I'd say it's an opportunity if you are ready for it. And I'd say it with a pinch of salt, because I also know I'm lucky to have a family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel capable. By graduation I'd have three years of running things, tutoring and a paperwork service for trades. I'd be among the few in my year with real customers and real revenue, and AI-skills on top. The risk is that thinking work gets so cheap that my service isn't worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the service now and sign up 10 local firms at 40 a month, maybe 400 a month. I'd save half of it. I'd study the tools every week, and watch for the moment the market gets too crowded. I'd probably look at buying a van or a small unit, something physical, so I own something that isn't software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Competitive and focused. Like preparing for an exam I know the date of. Some guilt, too, because I have help others don't, and I'd want to share what I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is your service getting too cheap. How would you protect against that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By owning relationships, not software. Local firms trust people they know, like me and Dad. And by adding something physical, like running a shared workshop or a storage space for trades. Software gets copied, but a van that's turned up at 8 a.m. for ten years has a reputation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for others, since you mentioned guilt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer free help to a few people, like my friend Daria's mum, who lost her bookkeeping job. I'd teach her how to use the tools to take on small clients. It's a small thing, but the parish would call it doing your bit, and I think that's right.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** to build something solid.
I'd say most people will **waste** it.
think: By graduation I'd have **real customers** and revenue, plus AI skills.
The risk is thinking work becoming so cheap my **service** isn't worth paying for.
do: **Sign up** 10 local firms at 40 a month.
**Save** half the income and watch for a crowded market.
**Buy** something physical, like a van or small unit.
feel: **Competitive** and focused, like an exam with a known date.
A little **guilt** about the help I have that others don't.
S3.quote: Software gets copied, but a van that's turned up at 8 a.m. for ten years has a reputation.
fieldNote: Plans to protect herself by owning **relationships and something physical**.
Her guilt becomes a parish-style act: teaching a friend's mum.
Uneasy because her own service could be undercut by cheap thinking work.

steps.text: Sign 10 local trades at 40 a month for paperwork help
Save half of the service income each month
Price a second-hand van or small storage unit
Teach a friend's mum to use the tools for small clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build a proper business and to teach young people how to cope with the change. I'd say it's an opportunity, and that governments should give people room to adapt rather than get in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel quite settled. By 28 I could have a decade of experience, a growing firm of my own, and a deposit. I'd also have a family by then, if things go as I hope. It's the version where my plan has room to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, run Dad's firm's office, and grow the paperwork service into a small company with staff. I'd invest early and keep studying tools as they come. I'd put money aside in a safe account too, for the part of the plan I can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, and a bit competitive. Like a long race where you can pace yourself. I'd still pray for those who'd get hurt, and I'd try to help the ones I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a family. How does the long timeline change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it possible. In the fast worlds I'd put it off, because I wouldn't know if I could pay for a child. Here I could marry in my mid-twenties, buy a small house, and still have time before the robots arrive in 2039. That's the thing that matters most to me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I get too sure of myself. I'd have been right about a lot of things, and that's when people make mistakes. I'd need Dad, or Father Tomas, to tell me when I'm wrong. Ten years of success isn't a reason to stop asking whether I'm wrong.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to build a **proper business**.
I'd say governments should give people **room to adapt**.
think: By 28 I could have a **decade of experience** and a growing firm.
It's the version where my plan has **room** to work.
do: **Graduate** and run the office side of Dad's firm.
**Grow** the paperwork service into a small company with staff.
**Invest** early and keep a safe account for the unseen.
feel: **Peaceful** and competitive, like pacing a long race.
I'd still **pray** for those who get hurt.
S4.quote: Ten years of success isn't a reason to stop asking whether I'm wrong.
fieldNote: Time makes **family plans** thinkable, which she says matters most to her.
Self-aware about overconfidence and names who would correct her.
Calm and ambitious, with faith as an anchor.

steps.text: Run the office side of Dad's plumbing firm after graduation
Grow the paperwork service into a company with staff
Put 100 a month into index funds and a safe account
Plan to marry and buy a small house before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It lands before I can build anything solid, and it hits my dad's customers, my degree and the plan all at once. What would help is the market staying open, a bit of breathing room for small firms, and families and churches ready to look after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people assume someone who uses AI all day is cold about it, but I care about the people who'd get hurt. I want to make sure the people I know are okay. I think that's what business should be for.

headlineQuote: People assume someone who uses AI all day is cold about it, but I care about the people who'd get hurt.
portrait: Vera is an **18-year-old** business student who tutors maths and does scheduling and invoices for her dad's plumbing firm.
She uses AI **every day** and treats change as a market process in which she can build something useful.
Her **traditional** side shows in her faith, her wish for family and a work-first view of debt and help.
Her dad's firm employs three men, so her **worry** is for their jobs and her parents.
She is calm in most worlds, anxious at 2028, and plans to protect others first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits her dad's customers, her degree and her plan together.
whatWouldHelp: **Breathing room** for small firms and a market that stays open.
Families and **churches** ready to look after each other.
